params.title: Aircraft
params.subtitle: How aircraft radios measure distance and direction, guide a landing, report to controllers, and call for help.

scenes.narration: Welcome to Aircraft. An airliner carries a whole family of radios. Some tell the pilot how far away a ground station is, or in which direction it lies. Some guide the aircraft down to a runway in fog. Others let controllers on the ground see who is flying where, or let the crew talk and call for help. A technician who works on these radios needs to know what each one does, how it works, which frequencies it uses and what antenna it needs. You don't need any background in electronics; we'll build each idea from the start. By the end, you'll be able to match every aircraft system to its frequencies, its operating principle and its antenna, and spot the trap answers the exam likes to use.

params.title: Frequency: how fast a radio wave vibrates

scenes.narration: First, a quick refresher on frequency. A radio wave is an electrical vibration that travels through space. Radios send and catch these waves with antennas: metal rods and wires. A wave's frequency is how many times it vibrates each second, measured in hertz: 1 hertz is 1 cycle each second. Radio waves vibrate very fast, so we use bigger units. 1 kilohertz is 1000 hertz. 1 megahertz is 1000 kilohertz, a million cycles every second. And 1 gigahertz is 1000 megahertz. Each aircraft system works in its own slice of frequencies, called a band, chosen for how those waves travel. Watch for this trap: a wrong answer often keeps the right digits but swaps kilohertz and megahertz. 190 kilohertz and 190 megahertz look alike, but one is 1000 times higher.

params.title: What each radio tells the pilot
rows: How far is the ground station?
Lined up with the runway, on the slope?
Who is that, and how high? (controllers)

onScreen: Which way to the beacon? ADF
scenes.narration: With those units in hand, let's meet the radios. A navigation aid is a radio system that helps a pilot know where the aircraft is, even in cloud or at night. Each one answers a simple question. How far is a ground station? Distance measuring equipment, or DME. Which direction am I from the station? The VOR, short for very high frequency omnidirectional range. Am I lined up with the runway, and coming down at the right slope? The ILS, the instrument landing system. Which way is that beacon, a simple radio transmitter on the ground? Automatic direction finding, or ADF. And for controllers on the ground, a transponder answers: who is that aircraft, and how high is it? We'll take them one at a time, starting with distance.

params.title: DME: time a question and its answer

onScreen: Ground station answers with its own pulses
scenes.narration: How can a radio measure distance? Imagine shouting to a friend across a valley and timing their shout back: the longer the wait, the farther away they are. DME works the same way. The aircraft sends pulses, short bursts of radio energy, as its question. That question is called an interrogation. The ground station answers with pulses of its own. Radio waves always travel at the same speed, the speed of light: just under 1000 feet every microsecond, a millionth of a second. So the round-trip time, there and back, converts straight into distance. For the exam, the main principle of DME is that a measurable amount of time is required to send and receive a radio signal through the Earth's atmosphere. Trap answers talk about voltages, frequency changes or phase; DME is purely about time.

params.title: Where the question goes: a VORTAC

onScreen: Aircraft DME uses the TACAN's distance part
scenes.narration: Where does the aircraft's question go? Often to a ground site that combines 2 systems. One is a VOR, which tells a pilot their direction from the station; we'll meet it properly soon. The other is TACAN, short for tactical air navigation, a military system that measures both direction and distance. Put them together and you get a VORTAC: VOR plus TACAN. Civil aircraft use the TACAN's distance part as their DME ground station, so 1 VORTAC site gives a pilot direction and distance together. The pilot tunes in the station they want to use; on the exam, that's called the selected station.

params.title: DME versus radar and Loran C
rows: Times a passive echo off the target
Compares signals from a transmitter chain

onScreen: DME: the station answers; time gives distance
Radar: a passive echo off the target
Loran C: signals from a chain of transmitters
scenes.narration: So DME is the radio navigation aid that finds the distance to a selected VORTAC station by measuring how long the radio signal takes to travel to and from the station. As wrong answers, the exam offers 2 other systems that also use radio timing. Radar sends out a pulse and listens for the faint echo that bounces off a target; the target itself doesn't answer. Loran C, short for long range navigation, compares the arrival times of signals from a chain of ground transmitters. Neither one times a question and its answer the way DME does. A fourth choice, Distance Marking, is simply made up.

params.title: Why the ground station waits 50 µs

blocks.label: Aircraft interrogates
blocks.note: Pulses sent to the ground station

blocks.label: Airborne DME
blocks.note: Subtracts the delay: travel time left

scenes.narration: Back to the ground station's answer, because there's a twist in it. The DME ground station doesn't reply the instant it hears an interrogation. It has a built-in delay, typically 50 microseconds, between receiving the interrogation and transmitting its reply. Why wait? When the aircraft is very close, an instant reply could arrive while the airborne unit is still transmitting, or while its receiver is still recovering from its own strong pulses, and the reply would be missed. So the delay allows operation at close range. Because the delay is always the same, the airborne unit simply subtracts it from the time it measured. What's left is the true travel time. On the exam, the delay is not for someone to answer the call, not to clear other traffic, and not for any mechanical hookup.

params.title: Slant range: the straight line down
rows: Almost the distance along the ground
Right over it, about 1 mile up

onScreen: Slant range: the direct, slanted line to the station
Far away: almost the ground distance
Overhead, 1 mile up: reads about 1 mile
scenes.narration: So what distance does DME actually measure? The radio signal travels in a straight line between the aircraft and the station. The aircraft is up at altitude and the station is on the ground, so that line slants downward. That's why the DME distance is called the slant range: the direct, slanted line from the aircraft at altitude down to the station. Far from the station, the slant range is almost the same as the distance along the ground. But fly right over the station about 1 mile up, and DME still reads about 1 mile, even though you're 0 miles away along the ground. On the exam, slant range is not a DME bearing, a glideslope angle or a localizer course width; the last 2 belong to the landing system we'll meet later.

Next, which frequencies does DME use? It operates from 962 to 1213 megahertz. Say the unit carefully: megahertz. That band sits around 1000 megahertz, which is 1 gigahertz, much higher than the direction and landing radios we'll meet next. On the exam, the wrong choices for the DME band are those other systems' bands, all of them lower. So picture DME up near 1 gigahertz.

params.title: DME tunes itself to the paired VOR/LOC
items: DME stations sit beside a VOR or a localizer (LOC)
Each VOR or LOC frequency has 1 paired DME channel
Select the VOR/LOC frequency, and the DME tunes itself
Not marker beacon or glideslope pairings

onScreen: DME beside a VOR or localizer
scenes.narration: DME has one more convenience. A DME station is usually built beside a VOR, as at a VORTAC, or beside a localizer, LOC for short: the part of the landing system that lines an aircraft up with a runway. Each VOR or localizer frequency is paired with 1 DME channel. So most airborne DME systems automatically tune their transmitter and receiver to the paired VOR/LOC channel. Select the VOR or localizer frequency, and the DME is set too, giving direction and distance from the same site. The trap answers pair the VOR or localizer with a marker beacon or a glideslope, landing-system parts we'll meet later. So, DME in one sentence: a timed question and answer that gives the slant range to the station.

onScreen: Trap: 329.15 MHz to 335.00 MHz is the glideslope
scenes.narration: DME tells the pilot how far. The next system tells which direction: the VOR, short for very high frequency omnidirectional range. Very high frequency, or VHF, is the band VOR stations use. Signals there travel in straight lines, like light, so they reach about as far as the horizon; that's called line of sight. Omnidirectional means the station sends its signal in all directions at once, so it serves aircraft all around it. Ground-based VOR stations transmit from 108.00 to 117.95 megahertz. That's megahertz, not kilohertz: on the exam, the same digits in kilohertz are a trap, far too low for VHF. Another trap is 329.15 to 335.00 megahertz, which belongs to the landing system's glideslope. And DME, from before, sits far higher, near 1 gigahertz.

params.title: Magnetic north, not true north
rows: The North Pole, under the North Star

onScreen: True north: the North Pole and North Star
Magnetic north: where a compass points
scenes.narration: To describe a direction, we need a starting point: north. But there are 2 norths. True north is the geographic North Pole, the point the North Star sits almost directly above. Magnetic north is where a compass needle points, and it's a different spot, some distance from the pole. Pilots steer by a magnetic compass, and their charts show magnetic courses. So, to match, all directions associated with a VOR station are related to magnetic north. Not the North Pole, and not the North Star. Directions are counted in degrees, clockwise from north, all the way round to 360: east is 90 degrees, and south is 180.

params.title: VOR radials: spokes from the station
labels: An aircraft somewhere east of the VOR station
Radial: a line drawn outward from the station in a magnetic direction
This one points magnetic east: the 090 radial
Radials, not quadrants, bearings or headings

onScreen: An aircraft east of the station
Radial: a line outward from the station
scenes.narration: With north fixed, we can name directions from the station. Picture the VOR at the center of this compass rose, a circle marked in degrees, with magnetic north at the top. Out to the east is an aircraft. How do we say where it is? Lines drawn outward from the VOR station in a particular magnetic direction are called radials. Think of them as the spokes of a wheel, one for every degree. This line points magnetic east from the station, 90 degrees, and radials are always named with 3 digits, so it's the 090 radial, and our aircraft is on it. The exam's trap words are quadrants, bearings and headings. A heading is the way the aircraft's nose points, and a bearing is the direction toward something. A radial always starts at the station and runs outward.

params.title: Carrying a signal: AM and FM
labels: Carrier: a steady radio wave at the station's frequency
AM: the carrier's strength rises and falls with the signal
FM: the carrier's frequency speeds up and slows down instead
In the VOR, each signal is a 30 Hz tone

scenes.narration: So how does the aircraft know which radial it's on? The VOR sends 2 signals and lets the receiver compare them. To follow that, we need 2 quick ideas. The first is modulation. A station's carrier is a steady radio wave at its assigned frequency. By itself, it carries no information. To add a signal, we vary it. In amplitude modulation, or AM, the carrier's strength rises and falls in step with the signal, as you see here. In frequency modulation, or FM, the strength stays steady and the frequency speeds up and slows down a little instead. The signal can be speech, or just a tone: a steady hum at one frequency. In the VOR, each signal is a low tone of 30 hertz: 30 rises and falls every second.

params.title: Phase: where a wave is in its cycle
labels: AC voltage: swings up and down, here 30 times a second
In phase: 2 waves peak at the same moment
Phase difference: how far one wave lags, in degrees

onScreen: AC voltage swings up and down
scenes.narration: The second idea is phase. In the aircraft's receiver, each 30 hertz tone becomes a voltage, the electrical push in a circuit. That push drives a current, a flow of electricity. This is an AC voltage, short for alternating current: it swings up and down, here 30 times a second, pushing the current one way and then back. Phase describes where a wave is in its cycle. We measure it in degrees: 1 full cycle is 360 degrees, like a full turn of a compass. When 2 waves rise and fall together, peaking at the same moment, they're in phase. If one peaks later, the phase difference says how far behind it is, in degrees. A quarter of a cycle behind is 90 degrees. Hold on to that; it's the heart of the VOR.

params.title: The 2 VOR signals
rows: From a rotating pattern: shifts with direction

onScreen: Reference phase: FM, 30 Hz, same everywhere
Variable phase: AM, 30 Hz, shifts with direction
In phase at 360 degrees North, magnetic
scenes.narration: Now we can put the VOR together. Picture a lighthouse whose beam sweeps around, and which flashes an all-round light at the moment the beam points north. Time the gap from the flash to the beam reaching you, and you know your direction. A VOR does the same with 2 signals at 30 hertz. The reference phase signal is frequency modulated, and its timing is the same in every direction: that's the flash. The variable phase signal is amplitude modulated and comes from a rotating antenna pattern, the shape of the antenna's strongest signal: that's the beam. The 2 are synchronized, or timed, to be in phase at 360 degrees North, the magnetic bearing position. North counts as 360, a full turn. So magnetic north is the starting point for every direction. Trap answers say 180 degrees South, or a true bearing.

params.title: Phase difference gives direction, not distance
items: The receiver compares 2 AC voltages: the 30 Hz variable and reference signals
Example: a 90 degree difference means the 090 radial
Their phase difference gives the aircraft's azimuth from the station
VOR gives no distance: that comes from DME, by timing

scenes.narration: That's the station's side. In the aircraft, the receiver compares the phase of the 2 tones, as AC voltages. Moving clockwise from magnetic north, the phase difference grows by 1 degree for every degree of direction. So a phase difference of 90 degrees means the aircraft is on the 090 radial, magnetic east of the station. This direction, in degrees around the horizon from north, is called the azimuth. That gives the main VOR principle: a phase difference between 2 AC voltages gives the aircraft's azimuth position in relation to the selected VOR station. Notice what VOR doesn't give you: distance, even though one trap answer uses the same phase wording. Another, about timing a signal, is the DME principle. And DC voltages, from direct current that flows steadily one way, play no part.

params.title: How fast the VOR variable signal rotates
steps: The pattern turns at 1800 rpm (per minute)
params.answer: 30 revolutions per second: the 30 Hz signal

scenes.narration: One more VOR number. How fast does that variable signal rotate? The antenna pattern turns at 1800 rpm, revolutions per minute: 1800 complete turns every minute. The exam asks for revolutions per second. A minute has 60 seconds, so divide by 60: 1800 divided by 60 is 30. The variable signal rotates at 30 revolutions per second. Does that make sense? Yes: each turn of the pattern makes 1 cycle of the variable signal, which is exactly why it's a 30 hertz tone. The trap answers are 60, 1800 and 2400. 1800 is the right number in the wrong unit: per minute instead of per second. So, VOR in one sentence: compare 2 tones to find your radial, counted from magnetic north.

params.title: The 3 parts of an ILS
rows: Left or right of the runway centerline
Above or below the glide path

onScreen: Localizer: left or right of the centerline
Glideslope: above or below the glide path
scenes.narration: Direction and distance bring an aircraft to the airport. The last few miles need something more precise: the instrument landing system, or ILS. It guides an aircraft down to the runway when cloud or fog hides the ground. An ILS has 3 main parts. The localizer tells the pilot whether the aircraft is left or right of the runway centerline. The glideslope tells whether it's above or below the glide path, the gentle downward slope to the touchdown point. And marker beacons mark checkpoints along the approach, the aircraft's final path in to land.

params.title: The localizer: a required ILS component
items: Deviation: how far off the line you are
Localizer: a required component of an ILS
Shows horizontal deviation from the runway's center
Altimeter, VHF radio, DME: separate systems

onScreen: Deviation: how far off the line
Horizontal deviation from the runway center
Not required: altimeter, VHF radio, DME
scenes.narration: Now the exam's question: which piece of equipment is a required component of an ILS? First, a word it uses: how far off the line you are is called deviation. The answer is the localizer: it shows the aircraft's horizontal deviation, side to side, from the center of the runway. The other choices name other equipment on board: the altimeter, which shows height, the VHF radio, and DME. Each is useful on an approach, but each is a separate system, not a required part of the ILS.

params.title: The localizer sits inside the VOR band

scenes.narration: Let's look at the localizer in detail, starting with its frequencies. The ILS localizer beam system, used to find the runway centerline, operates from 108.10 to 111.95 megahertz. Notice that this sits inside the VOR band of 108.00 to 117.95 megahertz, so the same VHF navigation receiver can tune both. Don't mix the 2 ranges up: the localizer's is the narrower one inside. And as always, megahertz, not kilohertz. A trap answer offers 329.15 to 335.00 megahertz, which belongs to the glideslope; we'll meet it shortly. Another uses gigahertz, 1000 times too high.

params.title: How the localizer marks the centerline

blocks.label: Localizer antenna
blocks.note: At the far end of the runway

blocks.label: Above and below the glide path

onScreen: Localizer antenna at the far end of the runway
150 Hz pattern on the other side
Both tones equal: on the centerline
Above and below the glide path: glideslope, not localizer
scenes.narration: How does the localizer show left or right? It produces 2 amplitude modulated antenna patterns that overlap along the runway's line, each carrying an audio tone: a tone low enough to hear. Left of the runway centerline, the pattern has a 90 hertz audio tone. Both patterns come from the localizer antenna, at the far end of the runway. Right of the centerline, the pattern has a 150 hertz audio tone. Where the 2 tones are equally strong, the aircraft is right on the centerline. The aircraft's receiver compares the 2 tones: if one is stronger, the aircraft is off to that side. On the exam, watch for a choice describing 2 patterns, one above and one below the glide path. Those belong to the glideslope, not the localizer.

params.title: What the localizer shows the pilot
items: Deviation left or right of the runway centerline
Needle centered: on the centerline
Not ground speed, and not wind speed along the runway
Up and down guidance comes from the glideslope

onScreen: Deviation left or right of the centerline
scenes.narration: In the cockpit, the result drives a needle. On a runway approach, the ILS localizer shows deviation left or right of the runway centerline. If the needle swings right, the centerline is to the right, so the pilot steers toward the needle until it's centered. That's all the localizer does: side-to-side guidance. It does not show ground speed, or deviation from an authorized ground speed, or wind speed along the runway. No part of the ILS measures those. And it doesn't show up and down either; that's the glideslope's job, so let's go there next.

params.title: The glideslope: up and down
items: Glideslope: above or below the glide path
Ground antenna beside the runway, 2 patterns compared
Signal: 329.15 MHz to 335.00 MHz
Paired with the localizer: select the localizer, and the glideslope tunes too

onScreen: Glideslope: above or below the glide path
scenes.narration: The glideslope does for up and down what the localizer does for left and right. Its ground antenna, beside the runway, sends 2 patterns, one above and one below the glide path, and the aircraft's receiver compares them the same way. A second needle then shows whether the aircraft is too high or too low. The glideslope uses higher frequencies, 329.15 to 335.00 megahertz. Each one is paired with a localizer frequency, so selecting the localizer tunes the glideslope too. One localizer trap answer has that backwards, claiming the localizer tunes itself when the glideslope frequency is selected.

params.title: The glideslope's aircraft antenna
items: Dipole: 2 equal metal rods, fed in the middle
Folded dipole: the ends joined by a second rod into a long, flat loop
ILS glideslope installation: folded dipole reception antenna
Often mounted in the nose

onScreen: Dipole: 2 rods fed in the middle
Folded dipole: a long, flat loop
scenes.narration: To pick up the glideslope signal, the aircraft needs its own antenna. The simplest antenna is a dipole: 2 equal metal rods, fed in the middle, where the cable connects. A folded dipole joins the outer ends with a second rod, making a long, flat loop. An aircraft's ILS glideslope installation uses a folded dipole reception antenna, often mounted in the nose. Reception means it only receives; the aircraft never transmits on glideslope frequencies. Trap answers include a balanced loop, which belongs to the marker beacons coming next, and a phased array, a ground antenna we'll meet later.

params.title: Marker beacons: checkpoints on the approach
items: Small transmitters along the approach path
Each beams its signal straight up
Passing overhead: a tone sounds and a light flashes
Outer, middle and inner markers: all on 75 MHz

onScreen: Overhead: a tone and a light
scenes.narration: The last ILS part is the marker beacons: small transmitters set along the approach path. Each one beams its signal straight up. As the aircraft passes overhead, a tone sounds in the cockpit and a light flashes, telling the pilot how far along the approach they are. There are 3: the outer, middle and inner markers. All 3 use the same carrier frequency, 75 megahertz. Remember, the carrier is the steady radio wave a station sends. Because the markers share it, 1 receiver fixed on 75 megahertz hears them all. So how does the pilot tell them apart?

params.title: Telling the markers apart: the tone

scenes.narration: By the tone. Each marker is 95 percent tone-modulated: its tone amplitude modulates the carrier, swinging the carrier's strength by 95 percent. The tones are 400 hertz for the outer marker, 1300 hertz for the middle, and 3000 hertz for the inner, so the pitch rises as you near the runway. Trap answers turn those tones into carrier frequencies, such as 400 megahertz for the outer marker, or give each airport its own marker frequencies. In short: 1 carrier, 75 megahertz, and 3 tones. So, the ILS: localizer for left and right, glideslope for up and down, markers for how far along.

blocks.label: Loop and sense antennas
blocks.note: Find which way the signal comes from

onScreen: Non Directional Beacon: same signal all around
Loop and sense antennas find the direction
scenes.narration: Back to finding direction, now with an older and simpler system: automatic direction finding, or ADF. On the ground sits a non directional beacon, or NDB: a transmitter that sends the same signal in every direction. So the beacon itself gives no direction; the direction finding happens in the aircraft. The ADF uses a loop antenna, a loop of wire that picks up a signal strongly or weakly depending on the direction it comes from. A loop alone can't tell whether the beacon is ahead or behind, so a sense antenna, which hears every direction equally, settles that. From those, the ADF swings a needle to point at the beacon.

marks.label: 108.00–117.95 MHz
marks.note: VOR, with the localizer inside: traps

marks.label: 190–1750 MHz
marks.note: Same digits in megahertz: a trap

onScreen: Trap: the VOR and localizer bands
scenes.narration: Now its frequencies. An aircraft's ADF equipment covers 190 to 1750 kilohertz. That's kilohertz, not megahertz: far below everything we've met so far. The VOR band, with the localizer inside it, sits up at 108 megahertz and above, and the exam offers those ranges as trap answers. The sneakiest trap keeps the same digits but changes the unit: 190 to 1750 megahertz. That's 1000 times too high. When you see ADF, think kilohertz.

params.title: Low frequencies follow the Earth's curve
rows: Ground wave: follows the Earth's curve
Over the horizon: hundreds of miles
Line of sight: to the horizon

onScreen: Low and medium frequencies: ground wave follows the Earth's curve
Over the horizon, several hundred miles
scenes.narration: Why use such low frequencies? Because of how they travel. ADF works on low and medium frequencies, measured in kilohertz. Signals there travel as a ground wave, which hugs the surface and follows the curvature of the Earth. So ADF antennas can receive transmissions that are over the Earth's horizon, sometimes several hundred miles away. Compare VHF, which we saw goes in straight lines and stops at the horizon: line of sight. On the exam, one trap says ADF is limited to line of sight and won't follow the Earth's curve; that's backwards. Another says a single sense antenna is enough; the ADF needs its loop antenna too. A third says broadcast stations can't be used; in fact, ordinary AM broadcast stations work fine.

onScreen: ADF needle points at the beacon
At night the ionosphere bounces signals back
Sky waves from almost any direction
scenes.narration: Ground waves give steady bearings by day. At night comes a problem called night effect. High above the weather is the ionosphere, a layer of electrically charged gas, energized by sunlight, that can bend radio waves back down to Earth. By day, its lowest part soaks up low frequency signals heading skyward. After dark, that lowest part fades away, so NDB signals going upward bounce off the ionosphere and come back down as sky waves, from almost any direction. They mix with the ground wave, and the ADF needle wanders. The trap answers say NDBs are switched off at night, ADF transmissions slow down, or dew collects on the antennas. None is true, and the ADF doesn't even transmit; it only receives. So, ADF: kilohertz signals that reach over the horizon, but wander at night.

onScreen: Mode C transponder: receives 1030 MHz, transmits 1090 MHz
Reply to the ground station on 1090 MHz
scenes.narration: So far the aircraft has done the listening. Now flip it around: how do controllers on the ground keep track of aircraft? Radar shows echoes, but an echo doesn't say who the aircraft is or how high. So aircraft carry a transponder, short for transmitter-responder: a radio that answers automatically when asked. It works with the air traffic control radar beacon system, or ATCRBS. A ground interrogator sends a coded question, in pulses, on 1030 megahertz. Transponders come in types called modes. A mode C transponder, which reports the aircraft's identity and its altitude, receives at 1030 megahertz and transmits its reply at 1090 megahertz. Using 2 frequencies keeps questions and answers apart. Don't reverse them: the question goes out on the lower number, 1030, and the answer comes back on 1090.

params.title: Pulse position modulation
labels: A reply: a train of short pulses
2 framing pulses mark the start and the end
Code pulses sit in fixed time positions between them
Mode C encodes its reply with pulse position modulation

onScreen: Code pulses in fixed time positions
scenes.narration: What does the reply look like? It's a train of pulses. The first and last are framing pulses, like bookends. Between them are fixed time positions. In each one, a pulse is either there or missing, and that pattern spells out a code: the aircraft's identity code or, in reply to a mode C question, its altitude. Because the information is carried by where the pulses sit in time, this is called pulse position modulation. So a mode C transponder encodes its transmission to the ATCRBS ground station using pulse position modulation. The trap answers include amplitude modulation at 95 percent, which belongs to the marker beacons, differential phase shift keying, which sends data by flipping a wave's phase, and a made-up Doppler encryption.

params.title: Mode S: selective, with collision avoidance
items: S for selective: every aircraft has its own address
Duplicates all the mode C functions
Adds mid-air collision avoidance capabilities, used by TCAS
Not primary radar, lightning detection or backup voice

onScreen: Mode S: each aircraft has its own address
Not radar, lightning detection or voice
scenes.narration: Mode C has a limit: every aircraft in the ground station's beam answers at once, and their replies can overlap. Mode S, where S stands for selective, fixes that. Each aircraft gets its own address, so a station can question 1 aircraft at a time and exchange data with it. In addition to duplicating the mode C functions, a mode S transponder can provide mid-air collision avoidance capabilities. It's the link used by TCAS, the traffic alert and collision avoidance system: equipment on the aircraft that questions other aircraft's transponders, works out whether any are on a collision course, and warns the pilots. The trap answers offer primary radar, long range lightning detection and backup voice radio. So: asked on 1030, the transponder answers on 1090, and mode S adds collision avoidance.

onScreen: Mode S PPM pulses: 1030 MHz directional pattern
scenes.narration: To finish the picture, we need the antennas and frequencies that carry all these signals. Start on the ground. A mode S ground station can use a phased-array antenna: a panel of many small antennas fed with carefully timed signals. Where their waves line up, they add into a strong beam; elsewhere they cancel. Change the timing, and the beam swings round electronically, with nothing moving. So a phased array forms a steerable beam, aimed one way: a directional pattern. When it transmits the pulse position modulation, or PPM, pulses of a mode S interrogation for an aircraft's TCAS, what does it radiate? A 1030 megahertz directional pattern. 1030, because interrogations go out on 1030. Directional, because that's what a phased array does. Not 1090, and not omnidirectional.

onScreen: VOR and localizer: 108.00 MHz to 117.95 MHz
HF: 2.000 MHz to 29.999 MHz, a trap
scenes.narration: Next, the frequencies we haven't met yet. Pilots need to talk, so begin there. Aircraft very high frequency, or VHF, communications use 118.000 to 136.975 megahertz, and worldwide up to 151.975 megahertz. Voice on these channels uses amplitude modulation, AM. Notice where that band sits: just above the VOR and localizer band, which stops at 117.95. Navigation is below 118 megahertz, and talking starts at 118. On the exam, the trap answers are the VOR range, the glideslope range, and 2.000 to 29.999 megahertz, which is the HF, high frequency, band used for long range radio.

params.title: Emergency Locator Transmitters (ELT)
items: ELT: switches itself on after a crash
121.5 MHz: the civil aviation emergency frequency
243 MHz: the military emergency frequency, twice 121.5
406 MHz: a digital distress message for satellites
The exam answer has all 3: 121.5, 243 and 406 MHz

onScreen: ELT switches on after a crash
scenes.narration: Some radios are only for emergencies. An emergency locator transmitter, or ELT, switches itself on after a crash and sends a signal that rescuers can track down. Aircraft ELTs operate on 121.5, 243 and 406 megahertz. 121.5 megahertz is the civil aviation emergency frequency. 243 megahertz is the military emergency frequency, and it's exactly twice 121.5, which helps you remember it. 406 megahertz carries a digital distress message picked up by search and rescue satellites. Rescuers home in on 121.5 and 243 to find the aircraft. The trap answers list only 1 or 2 of these frequencies. The right answer has all 3.

onScreen: Radio altimeter sends a signal down
scenes.narration: Like the radar we compared with DME, one more system works by echoes: the radio altimeter. An altimeter tells the pilot the aircraft's height. The ordinary one works from air pressure and gives height above sea level. The radio altimeter instead sends a signal straight down and compares it with the echo coming back from the ground, giving the height above the ground directly below. That matters most in the last moments of a landing. An aircraft's radio altimeter operates from 4250 to 4350 megahertz, the highest frequencies in this lesson, over 4 gigahertz. The trap answer 962 to 1213 megahertz is DME's band.

onScreen: VOR, localizer and VHF voice: 108.00 MHz to 136.975 MHz
DME 962 MHz to 1213 MHz; transponders 1030 and 1090 MHz
scenes.narration: Let's line up the aircraft frequencies we've met, lowest to highest. ADF is down in kilohertz, 190 to 1750. Then a jump to megahertz: VOR and the localizer from 108, then VHF voice from 118 to 136.975. The ELTs sit at 121.5, 243 and 406. Up near 1000 megahertz come DME, at 962 to 1213, and the transponders, receiving on 1030 and replying on 1090. And at the top, the radio altimeter, 4250 to 4350 megahertz. If a choice puts any of these in the wrong unit, it's wrong.

params.title: The transponder's antenna
items: Ground stations can be in any direction: it must be omnidirectional
Monopole: a single short rod standing out from the metal skin
Shaped as a small blade, usually on the belly
L-band: the frequencies around 1 GHz, where 1030 and 1090 MHz sit
Mode C: L-band monopole blade-type omnidirectional antenna

scenes.narration: Frequencies done; now the antennas on the aircraft, starting with the transponder's. Ground stations could be in any direction, so the transponder needs an omnidirectional antenna: one that hears equally well all the way around. It uses a monopole: a single short rod standing out from the aircraft's metal skin, which acts as the other half of the antenna. Shaped as a small swept blade, streamlined against the airflow, it usually sits on the belly. L-band is the name for the radio frequencies around 1 gigahertz, where 1030 and 1090 megahertz sit. So a mode C transponder receives its 1030 megahertz ATCRBS interrogation signals through an L-band monopole blade-type omnidirectional antenna. The trap answers are a phased array, which belongs on the ground, a folded dipole, which is the glideslope's, and a rotating loop.

params.title: The marker beacon antenna
items: Marker beacons beam their 75 MHz signal straight up
Heard only as the aircraft passes overhead
Aircraft antenna: a balanced loop on the belly
Receive only: the aircraft never transmits on 75 MHz

scenes.narration: Next, the marker beacon receiver. Remember that marker beacons beam their 75 megahertz signal straight up, so the aircraft only needs to hear them as it passes directly overhead. Its antenna sits under the belly, facing down toward the beacons. An aircraft's ILS marker beacon installation uses a balanced loop reception antenna: a flat loop of metal. Like the glideslope antenna, it only receives; the aircraft never transmits on the marker frequency. The trap answers name the folded dipole, which is the glideslope's, a steerable phased array, and a horizontally polarized omnidirectional antenna, which belongs to the VOR, as we'll see next.

params.title: VOR and localizer: horizontal polarization
items: Polarization: the direction a radio wave vibrates in
Vertical: up and down. Horizontal: side to side
VOR and localizer signals are horizontally polarized
Aircraft VOR/LOC antenna: horizontally polarized, omnidirectional

onScreen: Polarization: the direction the wave vibrates
scenes.narration: The VOR and localizer antenna depends on an idea called polarization. A radio wave, as we saw at the start, is an electrical vibration. As it travels, it vibrates in one direction: up and down for vertical polarization, side to side for horizontal. An antenna picks up a wave best when it lines up the same way. VOR and localizer stations send horizontally polarized signals, and the aircraft must hear stations in any direction. So aircraft VOR and localizer installations use a horizontally polarized omnidirectional reception antenna, often a V-shaped pair of rods on the tail. The trap answer is a vertically polarized antenna; that's what VHF voice radios use. Others offer a balanced loop transmission antenna or a folded dipole.

onScreen: Mode C transponder: L-band monopole blade, omnidirectional
VOR and localizer: horizontally polarized omnidirectional
scenes.narration: Here are all 4 aircraft antennas side by side, because the exam loves to swap them. The mode C transponder hears its 1030 megahertz interrogations through an L-band monopole blade, omnidirectional. The ILS glideslope uses a folded dipole. The ILS marker beacon uses a balanced loop. And the VOR and localizer share a horizontally polarized omnidirectional antenna. Read the question for the installation's name, then match it to its antenna.

blocks.label: Aircraft generator
blocks.note: Makes AC power, often at 400 Hz

blocks.label: Transformer
blocks.note: 2 coils on an iron core: changes voltage

blocks.label: Chokes and filters
blocks.note: Smooth the power into a steady supply

blocks.label: Radios and avionics
blocks.note: Run on the voltages they need

onScreen: Generator: AC power, often at 400 Hz
scenes.narration: That covers frequencies and antennas. Our final topic is the equipment itself: how it's powered, what microphones it uses, how much power it transmits, and a couple of practical systems. Start with power. Many aircraft generate AC, alternating current, which, like the AC voltages in the VOR, reverses direction many times a second. Aircraft AC power usually runs at 400 hertz, much faster than the 60 hertz of household power in the United States. The radios can't use it just as it comes: each needs its own voltages, so its power supply converts the aircraft power. A transformer, 2 coils of wire wound on an iron core, steps the voltage up or down. Chokes, which are coils too, and filters smooth the power, so the radios and other avionics, meaning aviation electronics, get a steady supply.

onScreen: 400 Hz: smaller, lighter transformers, chokes and filters
scenes.narration: Why 400 hertz? Transformers and chokes are magnetic devices: while the current flows one way, their iron core builds up magnetism, then lets it go. At 60 hertz, each one-way push lasts a long time, so a lot of magnetism builds up, and the core must be big and heavy to hold it. At 400 hertz, the current reverses more than 6 times as often, each push is short, and a much smaller core does the same job. So the principal advantage of 400 hertz line power is that magnetic devices such as transformers, chokes and filters are smaller and lighter than those used in 60 hertz power supplies. On an aircraft, weight matters. The trap answers say 400 hertz supplies draw less current, run cooler and more efficiently, or cost less. Size and weight are the real reason.

blocks.label: Voice
blocks.note: Sound waves push a thin diaphragm

blocks.label: Coil moves
blocks.note: Attached to the diaphragm, near a magnet

blocks.label: Small voltage
blocks.note: Made by the moving coil: the audio

scenes.narration: From the power supply to the cockpit: microphones. Aviation services use predominantly dynamic microphones. Inside one, a thin diaphragm, a flexible disc, moves back and forth as your voice hits it. A small coil of wire is attached to it, sitting near a magnet. When a coil moves near a magnet, a voltage appears across it, the same way a generator works. So the microphone turns sound straight into an electrical signal, with no battery or supply voltage needed. Aviation chooses them because they're rugged and tolerate vibration, humidity and temperature extremes, and a cockpit has plenty of all 3. The trap answers are carbon microphones, which are noisy and wear out, condenser microphones, which need a supply voltage, and piezoelectric crystal microphones, which are fragile.

params.title: Transmitter power: HF versus VHF
rows: Long range: sky waves across oceans
Line of sight reaches far from altitude

scenes.narration: The microphone's signal goes to a transmitter. How much power does it send out? RF output, RF being short for radio frequency, is the radio power a transmitter delivers to its antenna, measured in watts, the unit of power. Aircraft carry 2 kinds of voice radio. HF, high frequency, radios work from about 2 to 30 megahertz. Their signals bounce off the ionosphere as sky waves, as we saw with the ADF at night, so they can reach across oceans. That takes more power. VHF only travels line of sight, but from high altitude the horizon is far away, so less power is enough. Typical airborne HF transmitters provide a nominal RF output of 100 watts to the antenna, compared with 20 watts from a typical VHF transmitter. Nominal just means the rated, typical value. Keep the order straight: HF 100, VHF 20.

params.title: Before ground testing an aircraft radar
items: Aircraft radar sends powerful microwave pulses from the nose
That energy can injure people close in front of the antenna
First: clear the area in front of the antenna of other personnel
Equipment checks come after: people first

onScreen: Clear the area in front of the antenna
scenes.narration: One more transmitter needs special care: the radar. Many aircraft carry one, usually a weather radar in the nose. It sends out powerful pulses of microwave energy, radio waves of several gigahertz, and that energy can injure anyone standing close in front of the antenna. It heats body tissue the way a microwave oven heats food. So, before ground testing an aircraft radar, the operator should ensure the area in front of the antenna is clear of other maintenance personnel, to avoid radiation hazards. The other exam choices are sensible checks: shielding and grounding the receiver, testing the transmitter into a matched load, which is a dummy antenna that soaks up the power, or measuring power supply voltages. But they protect equipment. Protecting people comes first.

blocks.label: Flight crew alerted
blocks.note: No need to monitor the frequency

onScreen: Selected aircraft or group decodes it
Crew alerted without monitoring the frequency
scenes.narration: Our last system solves a tiring problem. On long flights over oceans, crews talk to the ground on HF radio, which is full of noise and static. Listening to it for hours is exhausting. SELCAL, short for selective calling, is a system where a ground-based transmitter can call a selected aircraft, or a group of aircraft, without the flight crew monitoring the ground-station frequency. Each aircraft has its own code of 4 tones. The ground station sends that code, and the aircraft's decoder recognizes it and sounds a chime. Until then, the crew can keep the noisy speaker turned down. Other aircraft aren't called. The trap answers describe calibrating selectivity, encrypting flight data, or calculating distances; SELCAL does none of these.

params.title: Key facts to remember
items: DME: a timed question and answer gives slant range; 962–1213 MHz
VOR: 2 signals in phase at magnetic north give direction, not distance
Localizer 108.10–111.95 MHz, 90 and 150 Hz; all 3 markers on 75 MHz
ADF in kHz, over the horizon; transponder receives 1030, transmits 1090 MHz
Glideslope folded dipole, marker balanced loop, transponder blade, VOR/LOC horizontal

onScreen: DME: slant range, 962 MHz to 1213 MHz
VOR: direction from magnetic north, not distance
Localizer 108.10 MHz to 111.95 MHz; markers 75 MHz
ADF in kHz; transponder receives 1030, transmits 1090
Match each installation to its antenna
scenes.narration: Let's wrap up with 5 things to remember. First, DME times a question and its answer to give the slant range, on 962 to 1213 megahertz. Second, VOR sends 2 signals that are in phase at magnetic north, and their phase difference gives direction, but not distance. Third, the ILS localizer, on 108.10 to 111.95 megahertz, uses 90 and 150 hertz patterns for left and right, and all 3 marker beacons share 75 megahertz. Fourth, ADF works in kilohertz and reaches over the horizon, while the transponder receives on 1030 and transmits on 1090 megahertz. Fifth, match each installation to its antenna: a folded dipole for the glideslope, a balanced loop for the markers, an L-band monopole blade for the transponder, and a horizontally polarized antenna for the VOR and localizer. And whatever the question, check kilohertz against megahertz.
